title: When Can Quantum Extreme Learning Machines Replace Quantum Reservoirs?
authors: Markus Baumann, Gerhard Stenzel, Jonas Stein, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien
abstract: Quantum reservoir computers (QRCs) retain information from earlier inputs, whereas reset-window quantum extreme learning machines (QELMs) start afresh and receive only a recent input window. We establish when this window can replace the reservoir's memory. Under our stated assumptions and with exact expectation values, sufficiently expressive QELMs can reproduce reservoir outputs arbitrarily accurately as their windows grow precisely when the influence of the omitted past becomes uniformly negligible. However, longer windows do not always solve the problem. We construct a simple two-qubit reservoir that performs temporal recall exactly, while every fixed-window predictor faces the same positive worst-case error over unbounded delays, regardless of model capacity. Analytical benchmarks and simulations distinguish missing history from limited features and finite measurements. The central conclusion is simple: better representations can improve how available information is used, but cannot recover a past the model never receives.
summary: This work determines the precise conditions under which a memory-limited Quantum Extreme Learning Machine can replace a quantum reservoir computer. The central finding is that perfect emulation requires the influence of the omitted past history to vanish uniformly, establishing a fundamental limit on what finite-window models can reconstruct about a system's true history.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental conditions under which a memory-less Quantum Extreme Learning Machine (QELM) can accurately emulate the temporal memory retention capabilities of a Quantum Reservoir Computer (QRC).
main_result: Accurate emulation is possible if and only if the influence of the omitted past history becomes uniformly negligible as the input window grows, otherwise, a persistent error floor remains regardless of model capacity.
method: The analysis compares the QRC output to the QELM prediction by quantifying the worst-case output variation ($D_d$) when the input window is fixed but the past history varies.
model_or_system: The models involve quantum reservoir dynamics (QRC) and reset-window QELMs operating on quantum states ($ho_t$). The dynamics are governed by input-dependent Hamiltonians and local dissipation terms.
key_observables: The primary observable is the error floor $D_d$, which quantifies the output variation due to missing history; other observables include the trace distance ($	ext{D}_{	ext{tr}}$) and the joint spectral radius ($	ext{r}_{	ext{vis}}$).
important_parameters: Window length ($d$), the decay rate characterized by $	ext{r}_{	ext{vis}}$, and the error tolerance ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes exact expectation values and focuses on the theoretical limits of representation capability, distinguishing this from practical training efficiency.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically compares QRC memory retention (state evolution) versus QELM window usage, illustrating cases where memory influence vanishes versus where a gap persists.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework by defining the memory difference between QRCs and QELMs, deriving the necessary condition for emulation ($	ext{D}_d 	o 0$), and then providing rigorous bounds and counterexamples using specific quantum models.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical boundary for using machine learning models (QELMs) to simulate physical systems with inherent memory (QRCs), which is crucial for understanding the limits of quantum machine learning in physics.

Orange denotes the QRC; blue denotes an ideal window prediction. These are schematic examples, not trained-model results: time advances while the window length stays fixed (Section 2).
